title: Pre-Modern Science
description: Babylonian, Greek, Islamic, and East Asian roots

concepts.title: Mesopotamia and Egypt
concepts.contentHtml:
The earliest systematic empirical knowledge: Babylonian astronomy (detailed observational records, prediction of eclipses); Egyptian mathematics (geometry for surveying, fractions, pyramid construction).

The Babylonians used a sexagesimal (base-60) number system that survives in our 60-second/60-minute time and 360-degree circle. They tracked planetary motions over centuries with remarkable precision.

These were largely empirical and pragmatic, not 'scientific' in the modern sense — but the data they collected was genuinely valuable.

concepts.title: Greek Natural Philosophy
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 6th century BCE, Greek philosophers asked theoretical questions about nature without (always) appealing to gods. Thales sought primal substances. Pythagoras saw mathematics as fundamental. Democritus proposed atoms.

Aristotle's systematic biology, physics, and logic shaped Western thought for ~2000 years. Euclid's Elements (~300 BCE) became the model of deductive reasoning. Archimedes (~250 BCE) combined mathematics with experimental physics — the lever, hydrostatics, mechanics.

Ptolemy's geocentric astronomy and Galenic medicine dominated until the Scientific Revolution.

concepts.title: Islamic Golden Age & Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Islamic civilization (~800-1400) absorbed, preserved, and extended Greek/Indian/Persian knowledge. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad translated Greek classics. Al-Khwarizmi founded algebra. Ibn al-Haytham revolutionized optics with empirical methods (controlled experiments, mathematical models).

Indian mathematicians (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, Bhaskara) developed Hindu-Arabic numerals, the decimal system, and the concept of zero — transmitted to Europe through Islamic intermediaries.

Chinese science was advanced in technology (paper, printing, gunpowder, compass) but more practical than theoretical. East Asian astronomy was very precise.

concepts.title: Copernicus & Heliocentrism
concepts.contentHtml:
Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus (1543) proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun. More elegant in some respects, though it still used epicycles and was not much simpler or more accurate than Ptolemy's geocentric model.

Tycho Brahe made the most precise pre-telescopic observations. Johannes Kepler used Brahe's data to derive his three laws of planetary motion (1609-1619): orbits are ellipses, equal areas in equal times, T² ∝ r³.

Galileo's telescopic observations (Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases, sunspots) provided strong empirical support. His advocacy of heliocentrism brought him into conflict with the Catholic Church (1633 trial).

concepts.title: The Scientific Method
concepts.contentHtml:
Francis Bacon (early 1600s) advocated systematic empirical observation and induction — knowledge built up from data rather than deduced from first principles. René Descartes complemented this with mathematical deduction and skeptical methodology.

The Royal Society (founded 1660) and the French Académie des sciences (1666) institutionalized scientific inquiry: regular meetings, journals, replication, open communication (formal peer review developed later, from the 18th century).

'The scientific method' is a useful idealization rather than a single procedure. Real science combines theory, experiment, observation, mathematics, and social institutions.

concepts.title: Newton's Synthesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Isaac Newton's Principia (1687) unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics under three laws of motion and universal gravitation. The same gravity that drops an apple holds the moon in orbit.

Newton's calculus (developed independently by Leibniz) provided the mathematical machinery. The clockwork universe — a deterministic, mathematical, predictable cosmos — became the dominant scientific worldview for ~200 years.

Newton's framework worked so well that some late-19th-century physicists thought physics was nearly complete. The 19th-20th centuries would prove otherwise.

concepts.title: Thermodynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
Steam engines drove industrial revolution. Sadi Carnot, Rudolf Clausius, and William Thomson (Kelvin) developed thermodynamics — laws governing heat, energy, and entropy.

The first law: energy is conserved. The second law: entropy of an isolated system increases. The conceptual revolution: heat is not a substance ('caloric') but a form of energy. The arrow of time has a thermodynamic origin.

Statistical mechanics (Boltzmann, Maxwell, Gibbs) connected microscopic particle motions to macroscopic thermodynamics. Chemistry and physics converged.

concepts.title: Darwin & Evolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) proposed natural selection as the mechanism for evolution. Co-discovered with Alfred Russel Wallace.

The shock was profound — humans, like other species, evolved from common ancestors. The mechanism (variation, inheritance, differential survival/reproduction) was clear and testable.

Mendel's pea-plant experiments (1866) established genetic inheritance, but were largely unrecognized until 1900. The 'modern synthesis' (~1930-50) combined Mendelian genetics with Darwinian evolution into the coherent neo-Darwinian theory.

concepts.title: Electromagnetism & Atoms
concepts.contentHtml:
Michael Faraday's experiments in the 1830s laid groundwork. James Clerk Maxwell's 1865 equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light. The discovery that light is electromagnetic radiation (and the calculation of its speed) was a triumph of theoretical physics.

John Dalton's atomic theory (early 1800s) was confirmed and extended. The periodic table (Mendeleev 1869) predicted undiscovered elements. By 1900, atoms were not in doubt — but their internal structure was unknown.

The discoveries of X-rays (Röntgen 1895), radioactivity (Becquerel 1896), and the electron (J.J. Thomson 1897) opened the way to 20th-century physics.

concepts.title: Einstein and Relativity
concepts.contentHtml:
Einstein's special relativity (1905) abolished absolute space and time. Time dilation, length contraction, and E = mc² followed from the constancy of the speed of light.

General relativity (1915) reformulated gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Predictions: gravitational lensing (confirmed 1919), gravitational waves (detected 2015), GPS clock corrections (used daily).

Newton's clockwork universe was overthrown. Yet Newtonian physics remains accurate at human scales — relativity's effects are tiny except at high speeds or strong gravity.

concepts.title: Quantum Mechanics
concepts.contentHtml:
Max Planck's blackbody quanta (1900), Einstein's photons (1905), and Bohr's quantized atom (1913) hinted at a deeper revision. Schrödinger and Heisenberg's quantum mechanics (1925-26) and Dirac's relativistic version (1928) gave a complete formalism.

Quantum mechanics is wildly counterintuitive: superposition, entanglement, uncertainty. But it predicts experiments to extraordinary precision — the electron's magnetic moment matches theory to 12 significant figures.

The interpretation of quantum mechanics remains debated. The Copenhagen, many-worlds, pilot-wave, and other interpretations all match experiment but tell different stories about what 'really' happens.

concepts.title: Molecular Biology
concepts.contentHtml:
Watson and Crick's DNA structure (1953) revealed how heredity is encoded. Genetic code cracked through the 1960s. Recombinant DNA (1970s), PCR (1980s), human genome (2003), CRISPR gene editing (2012) — biology became increasingly molecular and engineerable.

The 20th century saw biology move from descriptive to mechanistic. The 21st century is moving from understanding to designing. Synthetic biology, gene editing, and AI-aided design (AlphaFold) accelerate the trajectory.

title: Big Science & 21st Century
description: Scale, computation, and the changing nature of science

concepts.title: Big Science
concepts.contentHtml:
The 20th century saw the rise of big science — government-funded mega-projects involving thousands of scientists. Manhattan Project (atomic bomb, ~$26B in today's dollars). Apollo program ($280B). LHC (~$10B). ITER. James Webb Space Telescope.

Such projects achieve what individual scientists or labs cannot. They also involve their own politics, bureaucracy, and tradeoffs.

Cold War competition drove much 20th-century science funding. Post-Cold War science funding has stagnated relative to GDP in most Western countries.

concepts.title: Computation as Method
concepts.contentHtml:
Computers have become a third pillar of science alongside theory and experiment. Computational science simulates phenomena (climate, plasma, molecular dynamics) too complex for analytic theory or pure experiment.

Increasingly, machine learning is finding patterns and making predictions in domains too data-rich for humans to analyze directly. AlphaFold's protein structure predictions, climate modeling improvements, materials discovery — all powered by computing.

Some philosophers argue this represents a fundamentally new mode of scientific knowing: predictions without explicit theory, models too complex to fully understand. Whether this is 'real science' is debated.

concepts.title: Replication & Open Science
concepts.contentHtml:
The 'replication crisis' (especially since 2015) revealed that many published results — particularly in psychology and biomedicine — fail to replicate. P-hacking, publication bias, and methodological weaknesses contribute.

The open-science movement responds: pre-registration of studies, open data, open access journals, and replication studies as legitimate research output.

Other 21st-century shifts: rising importance of China in science output, citizen science, AI-assisted research. Science remains humanity's most powerful tool — but its institutions are being reshaped.
